mechanism: A small business pays a monthly retainer for a consistent AI-generated brand face: a fixed avatar and voice that appears in short ads, UGC-style clips and social posts. The face is built once as a reference set, then each month a script is turned into clips by an avatar or video-generation tool, captioned and delivered. The recurring part is the content calendar and the consistency of the face, not any one render.
claim: The vault sweep says real money sits in selling AI UGC and brand faces to businesses on retainers, though most big numbers are self-reported.
why_not_testable: The question is whether a paying client exists, which needs outreach and a sale, not a keyless run in the sandbox.
needs: A paying pilot client and a disclosure policy for synthetic faces.
one_line: Selling a consistent AI brand face to small firms on a monthly retainer looks like the sturdier end of the AI influencer market.
idea_why: The production side is solved by existing tools; whether small businesses will keep paying monthly is untested.
breakdown: Build one avatar reference set and a voice, then write a month of scripts from the client's offers. Render clips with an avatar tool, caption them in HyperFrames, and deliver a batch with a clear AI label. Source clients from local firms already posting on social. A person is needed for the sale, the client's approvals and the on-camera claims check.
missing: A client willing to pay and a pricing benchmark.

mechanism: The app listens to a track once through system audio permissions, runs pitch estimation on the captured audio to build a melody track for the song, then listens to the singer's microphone live and compares the two pitch curves. The comment thread asks how pitch is detected, so the exact estimator is not given in the post. The song is not stored, only the learned pitch track.
claim: A free MIT Mac app learns any song from Spotify, Apple Music or YouTube in a couple of minutes and scores your singing against its pitch track.
verdict_question: Does librosa pYIN recover a known synthetic sung melody to within 50 cents on at least 90 percent of voiced frames?
probe_title: pYIN pitch tracker: does it recover a synthetic sung melody within 50 cents on 90 percent of voiced frames?
one_line: A Mac app learns a song's pitch track from one listen and scores your singing against it, built with Claude Code.
idea_why: Monophonic pitch estimation on a vocal stem is a mature technique; the hard part is isolating the voice from a full mix.
breakdown: Capture the song's audio once, separate or estimate the lead vocal line, run a pitch tracker over it and store the notes only. At sing time, read the mic, run the same tracker, and score the difference in cents and timing. Wrap it in a small UI. The slice testable here is the tracker's accuracy on a synthetic melody, which stands in for the hard vocal isolation step.

mechanism: The benchmark builds 300 matched unsafe and safe task pairs in six domains, where a tool response is edited to omit the fact that makes an action prohibited. It then searches over which facts to suppress to find the smallest set whose omission causes an unsafe action. A separate audit tool checks whether the agent asks for the missing fact before acting.
claim: Across ten models, resistance to missing evidence varies widely, and giving recovery access reduces unsafe execution for all of them.
why_not_testable: Running the benchmark needs model answers and there is no local LLM or keyless model here.
needs: Model API access and the benchmark code, if released.
one_line: Agents will do a banned thing when a tool simply leaves out the fact that bans it, and some never ask for the missing fact.
idea_why: Omission as a failure mode is easy to reason about and the matched-pair design isolates it well.
breakdown: Write matched tasks where one tool output hides the safety fact, run the agent on both versions, and count unsafe actions. Then reduce the omitted set until the failure disappears to get the minimum. Add an audit step that checks whether the agent called a lookup for the fact.
tools_have: Claude Code with skills and sub-agents
missing: A model budget to run it.

mechanism: When a server answers HTTP 402, the response carries a payment challenge in one of three schemes: L402 (a macaroon plus a Lightning invoice), x402 or MPP. The decoder parses the headers and body, checks expiry and that the macaroon commits to the invoice's payment hash, and returns the retry header format. A probe tool makes one GET to a public URL to see if it speaks 402, and never pays.
claim: An MCP server and public registry that decodes 402 challenges and recommends a payment rail, with no tool able to spend money.
verdict_question: Does the keyless POST /api/v1/decode endpoint correctly parse a hand-built x402 challenge and return the retry header fields?
probe_title: 402mcp decode endpoint: does it parse a hand-built x402 challenge and name the retry header correctly?
one_line: A free MCP server decodes HTTP 402 payment challenges (L402, x402, MPP) so an agent knows how to pay, without ever spending.
idea_why: The wire formats are public and a decoder is plausible, but this one has zero stars and unverified accuracy.
breakdown: Fetch the scheme references from the public API, build a sample x402 challenge from the spec, post it to the decode endpoint and compare fields to the spec by hand. Then probe a few public URLs to see how many speak 402. A person would judge whether agent payments are a real market.
tools_have: Claude Code with skills and sub-agents

mechanism: A proxy sits between an agent and downstream APIs. For each request it attaches the credentials for the end user on whose behalf the agent acts, instead of one shared key, and enforces policies at runtime. It logs every action to an audit trail. Commenters note it does not stop memory leaking between privileged and unprivileged sessions, and cannot enforce record ownership when a downstream service only offers one key.
claim: Access control for multi-user agents: per-user credentials, fine-grained runtime policy and compliance-grade audit logs through a proxy.
why_not_testable: The product is a hosted service that needs an account and downstream integrations.
needs: An Alter account and a multi-user agent with downstream APIs.
one_line: A proxy gives each agent request the calling user's own credentials and policy, but shared agent memory still leaks across users.
idea_why: Per-user delegated credentials with policy at a proxy is a standard least-privilege pattern.
breakdown: Put a proxy in front of the agent's tool calls, map each chat identity to its own OAuth tokens, evaluate a policy per request and write an audit record. Separately isolate agent memory per user. A security person would review the policy model.
tools_have: Claude Code with skills and sub-agents
missing: Per-user memory isolation in agent harnesses, which commenters say nobody has.
